sections.title: Krillion scoring tiers and exact point values

blocks.text: Every accepted Krillion answer lands in one of six visible rarity tiers. The tier awards a fixed number of points; it is not a smooth percentage scale. Moving from Schooler to Rare doubles the value from 30 to 60, while moving from Deep Cut to One in a Krillion adds only 15. That uneven ladder explains why a secure Rare answer is often a better decision than gambling an entire prompt for the top label.

blocks.text: Read the jumps, not only the labels

Plankton to Too Clever gains five points. Too Clever to Schooler gains fifteen. Schooler to Rare gains thirty—the largest single jump. Rare to Deep Cut adds twenty-five, and Deep Cut to the maximum adds fifteen. Aiming for the Rare band is therefore a sensible centre of gravity: it captures the biggest step without demanding that every answer be uniquely obscure.

blocks.label: Accepted does not mean strategically strong
blocks.body: A ten-point Plankton answer is correct and valuable when the alternative is a blank. Use the tier as crowd feedback, not as a verdict on factual quality.

sections.title: Convert Krillion score into dive depth

blocks.text: The depth formula is exact: depth in metres equals total score multiplied by ten. There is no hidden bonus for a streak, no multiplier for answering quickly, and no extra conversion step. A 295-point result is 2,950 metres. A 445-point result is 4,450 metres. Seven maximum answers total 700 points, so the theoretical ceiling for a standard seven-prompt Daily Dive is 7,000 metres.
Use a ten-second result check

Drop one zero from the displayed metres to recover the score, or add one zero to the score to predict depth. This catches transcription mistakes when comparing runs. If the result card shows 3,300 metres, the seven tiers must sum to 330 points. The formula lets us audit examples without guessing from the visual position of the dive marker.

sections.title: What Krillion answer rarity does and does not measure

blocks.text: Rarity describes how the accepted answer sits within the game's response data for that prompt. It does not measure how difficult the fact is in every culture, how many search results it has, or whether the player is clever. A regional food may be common to one group and a Deep Cut to another. A famous supporting character may beat a franchise lead because fewer players reach for it first.

Prompt wording matters just as much as the noun. Ghana can be a perfectly valid country containing G and A, yet it may be a crowded response because the name is short and easy to retrieve. Guinea-Bissau and Papua New Guinea travel farther from the first instinct, but introduce more typing risk. The tier records the outcome of that tradeoff in one run; it does not promise the same value whenever the word reappears.

sections.title: Krillion rare-answer strategy: a four-level risk ladder

blocks.text: Choose a risk level after reading the prompt, not before the Daily Dive. A category we know deeply can support a specialist answer. A category we barely know should stay near the safe end. The four levels below make that choice explicit and stop one disappointing tier from pushing the next prompt into a reckless guess.

blocks.text: Spend confidence where knowledge is real

Our preferred profile is Level 2 for most prompts, Level 3 in genuine strengths, and Level 1 when recall is weak. Level 4 is not a normal scoring strategy. If the answer needs a paragraph of defence, the 25-second game is the wrong place to litigate it. The maximum upside over Deep Cut is only fifteen points, while rejection can cost the entire prompt.

Use five seconds remaining as an automatic downgrade. A Level 3 candidate that is not already typed becomes Level 2 or Level 1. This rule converts time pressure into a decision instead of a panic. A ten-point anchor adds 100 metres; an answer left in the field adds nothing.

sections.title: Real Krillion answers and video decision points

blocks.text: The best scoring examples include both wins and failures. In one recorded run, dango answers “food served on a stick” and earns 85 points, or 850 metres. It is a regional food with an ordinary canonical name and an exact category match: a model Level 3 answer. Rosie from The Jetsons works for a fictional robot because the player searches supporting characters rather than mascots.

blocks.text: The Greek-versus-Roman mistake is the most useful negative example. The player knows Seneca and correctly identifies him as a philosopher, but the qualifier ancient Greek makes the answer invalid. Diogenes would fit the requested tradition. This is why the risk ladder begins only after category parsing: a Level 3 name in the wrong civilisation is not a daring answer; it is a zero-value mismatch.

Dango demonstrates the opposite. The answer is neither misspelled nor dressed in explanation. It simply occupies a quieter part of a broad legal category. That is the pattern worth repeating: uncommon retrieval, conventional wording, immediate category proof.

A final score is a portfolio of seven decisions. One spectacular answer cannot compensate for several blanks as efficiently as a steady set of middle-tier results. Compare three profiles. The safe profile—seven Schooler answers—makes 210 points. A volatile profile with one maximum, one Deep Cut, and five Plankton answers makes 235. The enormous difference in drama produces only 25 extra points. A balanced profile with four Rare, two Schooler, and one Plankton makes 310.

blocks.text: Why completion raises the floor

Suppose a risky candidate has an uncertain chance of acceptance while a Schooler-quality answer is already available. The safe answer locks 30 points. The risky answer must be both accepted and placed high enough to justify losing that floor. Krillion does not publish enough probability data for a precise expected-value calculation, so practical confidence replaces fake mathematics: choose the higher tier only when category fit and spelling are already solid.

The balanced profile is our realistic target because it comes from repeatable choices. Four clean one-ring upgrades matter more than one miraculous maximum surrounded by rushed defaults. This also produces a calmer run; no prompt feels responsible for rescuing the entire score.

sections.title: Review a complete Krillion score without chasing losses

blocks.text: Review the result in category order, not emotional order. First mark rejections and timeouts, because converting a zero into any accepted tier has the largest dependable effect. Next mark Plankton answers in categories we actually knew; those are candidates for a one-ring upgrade. Finally, keep the Rare, Deep Cut, and maximum answers whose category fit was clean, but record the retrieval route rather than worshipping the word.

blocks.text: Do not chase yesterday's lost points on today's first prompt. Rarity changes with the question and response pool, and knowledge strengths move from category to category. Carry one mechanical improvement—read qualifiers first, build three candidates, submit by five seconds, or check autocorrect. That creates more depth over a week than trying to force a Deep Cut after a disappointing result.

items.question: What are the exact Krillion point values?
items.answer: Plankton is 10, Too Clever 15, Schooler 30, Rare 60, Deep Cut 85, and One in a Krillion 100 points.

items.question: How is Krillion depth calculated?
items.answer: Add the seven prompt scores and multiply the total by ten. A 330-point run reaches 3,300 metres.

items.question: What is the maximum Krillion Daily Dive score?
items.answer: Seven 100-point answers make 700 points, which converts to the theoretical 7,000-metre maximum.

items.question: Does answering faster earn more points?
items.answer: The visible scoring system awards the fixed tier value. Speed matters because it prevents timeouts and leaves recovery time, not because a fast accepted answer receives a separate bonus.

items.question: Will the same answer always have the same rarity tier?
items.answer: Do not assume that. The prompt wording and response environment matter. Treat recorded tiers as examples of a retrieval route, not permanent prices attached to words.

items.question: Is a rejected rare answer better than a common valid one?
items.answer: No. A rejected answer receives no rarity tier. A Plankton response still contributes ten points and 100 metres.

items.question: Which tier should we aim for most often?
items.answer: Rare is a strong practical target because the jump from Schooler to Rare is 30 points. Use Deep Cut candidates when category fit and spelling are already certain.

That short run is unusually valuable for scoring analysis because it includes a ten-point opener, an 85-point dango result, a strong supporting-character answer, a Greek-versus-Roman category error, and a common volleyball choice.

segments.heading: Rules, rarity goal, and a ten-point capital
segments.text: The player reads the seven-prompts-a-day rule and chooses Canberra for a national capital that is not its country's largest city. It earns ten points, showing that an answer can feel less obvious and still overlap with the crowd.

segments.heading: Vegetable prompt and dango Deep Cut
segments.text: The vegetable answer moves the dive deeper, then dango earns 85 points and 850 metres for food served on a stick. Dango is the cleanest example of specialist recall with an exact category match.

segments.heading: Rosie as a supporting fictional robot
segments.text: Instead of a headline robot, the player retrieves Rosie from The Jetsons. The move illustrates a repeatable route: search supporting characters inside a familiar franchise.

segments.heading: Seneca fails the Greek qualifier
segments.text: Seneca is a philosopher but Roman, not Greek. The discussion reaches Diogenes only after the mistake. This is the clearest proof that uncommon knowledge cannot rescue a category mismatch.

segments.heading: Common volleyball and the completed result
segments.text: Volleyball lands at the common end, Qatar is used for a state-religion country, and the run finishes better than 85 percent of that day's players. At 02:59 the video moves to a separate movie pack; later footage is not evidence for the standard Daily Dive.

takeaways: Do not infer rarity from how clever an answer feels; Canberra still earned ten points in this run.
Copy dango's structure: specific, conventionally named, and unquestionably inside the category.
Search supporting characters when entertainment prompts offer a broad legal pool.
Check nationality, era, and other qualifiers before committing specialist knowledge.
Stop using the video as Krillion evidence after 02:59, when it changes to another mode and then other games.
